title: Koko Eating Bananas
description: Binary search the ANSWER on [1, max(piles)]: find the minimum k such that `canFinish(k)` is true.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: Koko has `piles` of bananas and `h` hours. She picks one eating speed `k` (bananas per hour) at the start and uses it for every hour. Each hour she eats from one pile — if the pile has fewer than `k` bananas left, she eats those and stops for that hour (she doesn't move on to another pile). I need the minimum integer `k` such that she finishes all piles within `h` hours."

"Clarifying questions:"

• Is `h >= piles.length` guaranteed? (If not, there's no feasible `k` — every pile takes at least one hour even at infinite speed.)
• Are pile values bounded? That'll set the upper search bound.
• `k` must be a positive integer, correct? (Not fractional.)
• If multiple `k` values tie at exactly `h` hours, return the smallest, right?
sections.why: The `h >= piles.length` precondition is the one that quietly makes the problem solvable — it's worth confirming because it's also why the upper bound on `k` is `max(piles)` (any faster and a pile still takes exactly 1 hour). The integer-k clarification matters because it tells you you're searching over `[1, max(piles)]`, not a real interval — that determines whether BS-on-the-answer is even the right family.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n * max(piles)) solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: try every speed from 1 upward. For each `k`, compute total hours as `sum(ceil(p / k) for p in piles)`. Return the first `k` where the total is `<= h`. That's O(n * max(piles)) — for each of up to `max(piles)` candidate speeds we do an O(n) feasibility check. With piles up to 10⁹, that's untenable."

"But notice the structure of what I'm doing: I'm scanning the answer space `[1, max(piles)]` looking for the smallest `k` that satisfies a predicate. If that predicate has the right shape, I can binary-search the answer space and skip from O(max(piles)) to O(log max(piles)) on the outer loop."
sections.why: This brute force is the bridge — it has to be stated as 'scanning the *answer space*' rather than 'scanning the *array*,' because that's the conceptual leap. Once you frame it as 'I'm searching for an integer that satisfies a monotone predicate,' BS-on-the-answer feels inevitable rather than magic. The phrasing matters: candidates who say 'use binary search' without saying 'on what' fail to communicate the actual insight.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What property of the predicate unlocks binary search on the answer?
sections.say:
"This is binary-search-on-the-answer — also called parametric binary search. The trigger: I'm looking for the minimum value of a parameter `k` such that a feasibility function `canFinish(k)` returns true. BS applies because the predicate is **monotone in k** — if Koko can finish at speed `k`, she can also finish at any speed `k' > k` (faster never hurts). So the sequence `canFinish(1), canFinish(2), ..., canFinish(max(piles))` is a string of `false`s followed by a string of `true`s. That's the exact shape BS converges on — find the boundary."

"The monotonicity is the prerequisite, just like 'sorted array' is for plain BS. The 'array' here is the implicit one indexed by k, and 'sorted' is the predicate's monotonicity. Same skeleton, just the search space is conceptual."

"Template choice: half-open `while (l < r)` with `r = m` on success and `l = m + 1` on failure — converges to the leftmost true, which is exactly the minimum feasible `k`."
sections.why: Naming the monotonicity explicitly is the entire derivation — without it, 'binary search on the answer' is a memorized trick instead of a principled application. The 'sorted array → monotone predicate' analogy is the one that generalizes to every parametric-BS problem (Capacity to Ship, Split Array Largest Sum, Aggressive Cows), so it's worth saying out loud — it's the transferable insight, not a problem-specific trick.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace these to make sure the feasibility function and the convergence are both right." Three cases — a standard mid-range answer, a case where the answer is large (forces the upper end of the range), and a degenerate all-ones case.

examples.note: Standard case — answer sits in the middle of the range.
examples.trace:
lo=1 hi=11
m=6 canFinish(6): ceil(3/6)+ceil(6/6)+ceil(7/6)+ceil(11/6) = 1+1+2+2 = 6 <= 8 ✓ → hi = 6
lo=1 hi=6
m=3 canFinish(3): 1+2+3+4 = 10 > 8 ✗ → lo = 4
lo=4 hi=6
m=5 canFinish(5): 1+2+2+3 = 8 <= 8 ✓ → hi = 5
lo=4 hi=5
m=4 canFinish(4): 1+2+2+3 = 8 <= 8 ✓ → hi = 4
lo=4 hi=4 → converged → return 4 ✓

examples.note: Tight schedule — h equals piles.length+1, so the answer is forced high.
Degenerate — answer is the lower bound of the range.
examples.trace: lo=1 hi=1 → loop never enters (lo < hi is false) → return 1 ✓

sections.why: The first trace exposes the subtlety: `canFinish(5)` returns true and we set `hi = 5`, then `canFinish(4)` ALSO returns true and we set `hi = 4`. The half-open template keeps pulling `hi` down to find the leftmost true, even when the predicate keeps succeeding. The third trace defends the loop condition — with `[1,1,1,1]` the answer is 1, and `while (l < r)` correctly skips the loop and returns the initial `l`. With `while (l <= r)` the loop would enter, compute `m = 1`, do unnecessary work, and could infinite-loop without careful bounds. The convergence pattern (`hi = m` on success, `lo = m + 1` on failure) is the one to memorize for leftmost-true.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• `h == piles.length` → minimum feasible `k` is `max(piles)` (one pile per hour at the slowest speed that still finishes the biggest pile in one hour).
• `h` very large (>> sum of piles) → answer is 1 (eat one banana per hour, never miss).
• Single huge pile (e.g. `piles=[10⁹], h=2`) → answer is `⌈10⁹/2⌉ = 500000000`. The upper bound `max(piles)=10⁹` is essential — without it the search space is wrong.
• Integer-division vs ceiling — must use `Math.ceil`, not `Math.floor`. A pile of 7 bananas at speed 3 takes 3 hours (not 2), because the last hour she only eats 1 banana but the hour is still consumed.
• Empty piles → not possible by problem constraints, but defensively `Math.max(...[])` returns `-Infinity`, so a guard might be warranted.
• `(l + r) / 2` overflow → safe in JS (Number is 64-bit float), but in C++/Java I'd write `l + ((r - l) >> 1)`.
sections.why: The single-huge-pile edge is the one to mention — it justifies why the upper bound is `max(piles)`, not `sum(piles)` (a common wrong guess). The ceiling-vs-floor edge is the load-bearing semantic bug; getting it wrong silently passes some tests and fails others, which is exactly the kind of mistake that's painful to debug in an interview. The overflow flag is the senior-tier touch.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n log M) where `M = max(piles)`. The outer binary search runs O(log M) iterations, and each one calls `canFinish` which is O(n) (sum a `ceil` per pile). So O(n log M) total.

Space is O(1) — just the pointers and the loop locals, no auxiliary structure.

The defense against pushback like 'but you have an O(n) function inside an O(log M) loop, isn't that just O(n * M)?' is: the OUTER loop runs `log M` times, not `M` times, because of the halving — each iteration kills half the candidate-speed range. So `log M` outer × `n` inner = `n log M`, much smaller than `n * M`.

If you wanted to extend: same template fits Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (search the answer space of ship capacities, predicate is 'does this capacity finish in <= D days'), Split Array Largest Sum (search the answer space of max-subarray-sum, predicate is 'can I split into <= K subarrays each with sum <= this?'), and Aggressive Cows (search the answer space of minimum gap, predicate is 'can I place K cows with gap >= this?'). All same skeleton: monotone predicate → BS the answer."
sections.why: The 'log M not M' clarification is the exact pushback interviewers throw because the loop syntax LOOKS like a linear scan over candidate speeds. Articulating that the outer loop is BS, not iteration, is what defends the bound. Naming the family of problems unprompted is the bonus — Capacity To Ship, Split Array Largest Sum, Aggressive Cows are all the same template, and showing you see them as a family is what proves you can apply this in a new problem you haven't memorized.

walkthrough.intro: Step through binary-search-on-the-answer. The search range is [lo, hi] over candidate eating speeds k; for each midpoint we compute total hours and check feasibility. The state panel shows lo, hi, mid (candidate speed), and hours (the feasibility computation).
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — piles=${JSON.stringify(piles)}, h=${h}`, state: { piles, h } };
yield { line: 3, label: `init answer-space lo=1, hi=max(piles)=${hi}`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi } };
for (const p of piles) hours += Math.ceil(p / k);
yield { line: 4, label: 'define canFinish(k): sum of ceil(p/k) for each pile, true if total <= h', state: { piles, h, lo, hi } };
yield { line: 10, label: `loop check: lo=${lo} < hi=${hi} → enter`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi } };
yield { line: 11, label: `mid = floor((${lo}+${hi})/2) = ${mid} (candidate speed)`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi, mid } };
yield { line: 12, label: `canFinish(${mid}): ${breakdown} = ${hours}, ${hours} <= ${h} → ${ok}`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi, mid, hours, ok } };
yield { line: 12, label: `speed ${mid} works → try slower: hi = mid = ${hi}`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi, mid, hours } };
yield { line: 13, label: `speed ${mid} too slow → must go faster: lo = mid+1 = ${lo}`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi, mid, hours } };
yield { line: 15, label: `loop ended (lo=hi=${lo}) — minimum feasible speed is ${lo}`, state: { piles, h, lo, hi, returns: lo } };

reference.approach: Binary search on the answer (monotone predicate)
notes: You're binary-searching the answer space, not an index in piles. The predicate `canFinish(k)` is monotonic: false for small k, true for large k.
Use the half-open pattern `while (l < r)` with `r = m` on success and `l = m + 1` on failure — converges on the leftmost true.
`Math.ceil(p / k)` is correct: any leftover banana in a pile costs a whole hour.
reference.crux: Binary-search the ANSWER — eating speed k in [1, max(piles)] — using the monotone predicate `canFinish(k)`: false for slow speeds, true for fast, find the boundary.
cruxDistractors: Linearly try every speed from 1 upward, returning the first k where total hours `<= h`.
Binary-search the sorted piles array for the pile size that makes the hours come out to exactly h.
Compute `ceil(sum(piles) / h)` directly — total bananas over hours gives the needed speed in one shot.

alternates.label: Linear scan (brute force)
alternates.when: The brute force to name before you discard it. Try every speed from 1 up to max(piles) and return the first that finishes in time. Correct but O(n·max(piles)) — untenable when piles can reach 10⁹. Only use this as the stepping-stone that motivates BS-on-the-answer.
notes: Scanning k from 1 upward hits the minimum feasible speed first because canFinish is monotone — same monotonicity the BS version exploits.
The outer loop runs up to max(piles) times; binary search collapses that to log(max(piles)) iterations.
State this out loud, then say 'the answer space is monotone — I can binary-search it' to motivate the optimal solution.

options: An index into the piles array
The answer space: candidate eating speeds k from 1..max(piles)
The hours h, looking for the smallest h that admits a feasible k
The pile sizes after sorting, looking for the median pile
questions.explain: `l` and `r` are speeds, not positions — they start at 1 and `Math.max(...piles)`. `piles` is only ever read inside `canFinish`, and it never has to be sorted.

questions.q: Why does this work — what property must the predicate have?
options: It must be O(1) so the inner loop doesn't dominate
It must be monotonic: once k is fast enough, every larger k also works
It must be symmetric — `canFinish(k) === canFinish(max-k+1)` — so midpoint reflection is valid
The piles must be sorted so canFinish can short-circuit on the largest pile first
questions.explain: Eating faster never costs more hours, so `canFinish` is false for every speed below the answer and true for every speed at or above it. That false-then-true boundary is the same shape sortedness gives plain binary search — `canFinish` being O(n) costs time but doesn't affect correctness.

options: `floor` would round 1.0 down to 0 due to JS float drift, undercounting hours on exactly-divisible piles
A partial pile still takes a full hour to finish
`ceil` matches the C++/Java integer division semantics the problem assumes
`floor` would count the FIRST hour of each pile as 0, off-by-one across all piles
questions.explain: Koko can't move to another pile inside the same hour, so the leftovers cost a whole hour: 7 bananas at speed 3 is 3 hours, while `Math.floor(7 / 3)` would claim 2. Undercounting hours lets a too-slow speed pass — the floor variant returns 3 instead of 4 on `[3,6,7,11], h=8`.

options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n * max(piles))
O(n * log(max(piles)))
questions.explain: The loop halves the speed range `[1, max(piles)]`, so it runs about log₂(max(piles)) times — not max(piles) times — and each iteration's `canFinish` walks all n piles once.

questions.q: Why is the search range upper bound `max(piles)` and not `sum(piles)`?
options: To save memory
At speed max(piles), even the biggest pile takes exactly 1 hour — no larger speed ever finishes faster, so it is the slowest speed worth considering
Because sum(piles) overflows
Because the array is sorted
questions.explain: Eating speed is capped meaningfully at the largest pile: any faster still clears that pile in one hour, so max(piles) is the true upper bound.

questions.q: The loop uses the half-open form `while (l < r)` with `r = m` on success and `l = m + 1` on failure. Why not `r = m - 1` on success?
options: `r = m - 1` would make the range `[l, m-1)` half-open the wrong way — it must be closed on the right
Because m itself might be the minimum feasible speed; `r = m` keeps m as a candidate, while `r = m - 1` could skip the answer
`r = m - 1` paired with `while (l < r)` can cause `r` to go below `l` on small ranges, terminating before convergence
Because m is computed via `floor` and is always one less than the true midpoint, so `m - 1` double-decrements
questions.explain: We're finding the leftmost true; a feasible m must stay in the range, so we shrink to [l, m], not [l, m-1].

questions.q: What does it mean to 'binary search the answer' here, as opposed to ordinary binary search?
options: You sort the piles first, then binary search them as the input array
You search over candidate ANSWERS (eating speeds) using a monotone feasibility predicate, instead of searching for a value inside the input array
You binary search the hours array — bisect on h until the predicate flips
You binary-search a precomputed hours-per-speed lookup table built in one pass
questions.explain: The 'array' is the implicit conceptual range of speeds 1..max(piles); the predicate canFinish(k) supplies the monotone ordering BS needs.

questions.q: If you replaced `canFinish` to return whether hours `< h` instead of `<= h`, what breaks?
options: Nothing — the loop converges to the same answer because `r = m` on success absorbs the off-by-one
Speeds that finish in exactly h hours would be rejected, so the returned minimum speed would be too large (or no answer found when h is tight)
The returned speed would be too SMALL by exactly 1 — you'd need to add 1 at the end
The loop would no longer terminate when `l + 1 === r`
questions.explain: Finishing in exactly h hours is allowed, so the predicate must use <=; using < discards valid speeds and inflates the answer.

questions.q: Which OTHER problem uses this identical 'binary search on the answer' template?
options: Two Sum — binary search for `target - nums[i]` in the sorted-array variant
Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days — search the answer space of ship capacities with a 'finishes in <= D days' predicate
Merge Intervals — binary search for the insertion point of each new interval
Search in Rotated Sorted Array — binary search the answer space of pivot positions
questions.explain: Capacity To Ship, Split Array Largest Sum, and Aggressive Cows all share the monotone-predicate-on-the-answer skeleton.

blanks.hint: upper bound of the answer space
round up — partial pile still costs an hour
keep m as a candidate when it works

L3.prompt: Write `minEatingSpeed(piles, h)` returning the minimum k bananas/hour Koko needs to finish all piles in h hours. Log `minEatingSpeed([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 6)`.
hints: Predicate canFinish(k) sums Math.ceil(p / k) and checks <= h.
